### Problem: Squares of a Sorted Array {#sec-tp-p3-b}

::: {.p-statement}
An array $a$ sorted in non-decreasing order, $1 \le n \le 10^4$, $-10^4 \le a_i \le 10^4$. Return an array of the squares of each number, **also sorted in non-decreasing order**. The follow-up asks for $O(n)$ time instead of squaring and sorting.

Source: [LC 977 · Squares of a Sorted Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/squares-of-a-sorted-array/){.solved difficulty="Easy"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Squaring is monotone on magnitude, not on value: $(-9)^2 > 4^2$. A sorted array's squares are *largest at the two ends* (a long negative tail and a positive head) and smallest near zero in the middle. So the sorted result is built by repeatedly taking the **larger** of the two end squares and dropping it at the back of the output — the @sec-tp-p3-a back-fill again, this time with the two "runs" being the array's two ends.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Square and sort.** `[x*x for x in a]` then sort. $O(n\log n)$ — simple, correct, but ignores the promise of $O(n)$.
2. **Two ends, fill from the back.** $\mathit{lo}=0$, $\mathit{hi}=n-1$, write position $p=n-1$; compare the end squares, place the larger at $p$, shrink that end. $O(n)$.

**Invariant.** At every step the $n-1-p$ largest squares are already in their final positions in $\mathit{out}[p+1 \dots]$, and the still-unplaced squares all lie in $a[\mathit{lo} \dots \mathit{hi}]$ — whose biggest square is one of the two ends.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Square and sort

::: {.form-next}
One list comprehension and `sorted`. $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ output. Interviewers accept it, then ask for the $O(n)$ the constraints promised — which is where the two-pointer falls out of the "sorted by magnitude at the ends" observation.

**Worked example.** nums $= [-4, -1, 0, 3, 10]$. Squaring each value gives $16, 1, 0, 9, 100$; sorting those gives $[0, 1, 9, 16, 100]$. Notice the squares are *not* already sorted ($(-4)^2 = 16$ sits before $0$) — that is exactly why a sort (or the smarter form 2) is needed.
:::

```{python}

    assert str(final) == "[0, 1, 9, 16, 100]"
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def sorted_squares_brute(nums):
    return sorted(x * x for x in nums)
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - square-and-sort baseline
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;
vector<int> sortedSquaresBrute(vector<int> a) {
    for (int& x : a) x *= x;
    sort(a.begin(), a.end());
    return a;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `x * x for x in nums` is a generator that squares every element in place order, and `sorted(...)` collects those squares into a list ordered small-to-large. It makes no use of the input being sorted, so it pays the full $O(n\log n)$ sort — the very cost form 2 removes.

#### Two ends, fill from the back

::: {.form-next}
Read the ends, place the larger square at the far right, step inward. Because you always take the current maximum, the output fills correctly from the back with no post-processing — the same "vacated tail" trick as @sec-tp-p3-a. This is $O(n)$ and is the answer the constraint is fishing for.

**Why the two ends, in plain words.** Squaring measures *distance from zero*, not value. In a sorted array the numbers farthest from zero are at the far left (most negative) and far right (most positive); the middle sits near zero. So the **largest square still unplaced is always one of the two end squares** — compare them, and the bigger one is the next entry of the sorted output, which we fill right-to-left.

**Worked example.** nums $= [-4, -1, 0, 3, 10]$. $\mathit{lo}=0$ (square $16$), $\mathit{hi}=4$ (square $100$): $100$ wins, write it at slot $4$, $\mathit{hi}\to3$. $16$ vs $3^2=9$: $16$ wins, slot $3$, $\mathit{lo}\to1$. $(-1)^2=1$ vs $9$: $9$ wins, slot $2$, $\mathit{hi}\to2$. $1$ vs $0^2=0$: $1$ wins, slot $1$, $\mathit{lo}\to2$. $0$ vs $0$: tie, slot $0$. Output $[0, 1, 9, 16, 100]$ — no sort needed.
:::

```{python}

#| renderings: [light, dark]

    assert str(final) == "[0, 1, 9, 16, 100]"

V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-squares-sorted
def sorted_squares(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    out = [0] * n
    lo, hi, p = 0, n - 1, n - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        a, b = nums[lo] * nums[lo], nums[hi] * nums[hi]
        if a >= b:
            out[p] = a; lo += 1
        else:
            out[p] = b; hi -= 1
        p -= 1
    return out

for _ in range(500):
    nums = sorted(random.randint(-9, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 10)))
    assert sorted_squares(nums) == sorted_squares_brute(nums)
assert sorted_squares([-4, -1, 0, 3, 10]) == [0, 1, 9, 16, 100]   # the board sample
assert sorted_squares([-7, -3, 2, 4]) == [4, 9, 16, 49]
assert sorted_squares([0]) == [0]
print("sorted_squares OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

vector<int> sortedSquares(vector<int>& a) {
    int n = (int)a.size();
    vector<int> out(n);
    int lo = 0, hi = n - 1, p = n - 1;
    while (lo <= hi) {
        long long l = 1LL * a[lo] * a[lo], r = 1LL * a[hi] * a[hi];
        if (l >= r) { out[p] = (int)l; ++lo; }
        else        { out[p] = (int)r; --hi; }
        --p;
    }
    return out;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `out = [0] * n` pre-allocates the answer so we can write any slot by index. `lo, hi, p = 0, n - 1, n - 1` puts read fingers at both ends and the write pointer at the far right. `while lo <= hi` (note $\le$, not $<$) keeps going until the fingers cross, so the single middle element is still placed. Each round computes both end squares `a` and `b`; `if a >= b` writes `a` at `p` and advances `lo`, else writes `b` and retreats `hi` — the `>=` gives a deterministic tie-break. `p -= 1` always moves left, filling the output from largest to smallest.

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Square and sort** is $O(n\log n)$ time, $O(n)$ output. **Two ends, fill from the back** is $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ output (no extra space beyond the answer) — one comparison and one pointer move per slot. In C++ note `1LL * a[hi] * a[hi]`: $10^4 \cdot 10^4 = 10^8$ still fits in `int`, but a signed multiply of two `int`s is UB bait the moment constraints grow (@sec-arr-cost).
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- All negative $[-5,-3,-1]$: the "larger square" is always the left end; output $[1,9,25]$ — the loop degenerates to a clean left-to-right read placed right-to-left.
- All non-negative $[1,2,3]$: mirror image; always the right end. Either way `lo <= hi` (not `<`) so the middle element is placed when the ends meet.
- $n = 1$: single iteration places it.
:::
